newsitem.title: FINLAND: Sun sees competitive edge in race for 2000.
newsitem.headline: Sun sees competitive edge in race for 2000.

text.p: Sun Microsystems Inc Chief Executive Scott McNealy said on Sunday the Java programming language gives his company a competitive edge in the race to re-engineer computer systems in the run-up to the year 2000.

"I think in the next couple of years you're going to see a lot of people re-engineer for the year 2000 by going to a Java-based environment," he told reporters after a one-day visit to unspecified Finnish clients.

Companies are moving away from mainframes to client server computer designs for 2000, he said, but alleged the Microsoft Windows NT system, one type of client server system, was not ready to be installed in large-scale settings.

"In three to four years from now NT might actually be ready and we might have some competition," he said. "I'm really incredibly excited that we are already in 1997," he said, citing delays in the release of version 5.0 of Microsoft's NT.

The millenium "bomb" -- when millions of processors may fail through an inability to handle the changeover to the new century -- offers opportunities for companies needing to overhaul their systems to migrate to Java, the programming language Sun developed and gave away to ensure worldwide compatibility on any computer, he said.

He was presenting Sun's vision of a future computing marketplace where "mere mortals" have no use for "personal mainframes" but instead download only the applications they need onto simple processors in a fully compatible network.
"Sun plans on being a fairly aggressive player in this new environment," he said. "There's no reason today to take any of your corporate information and lock it up in a proprietary mail format.
"Every time you type a bit of intellectual property into a Word format, (Microsoft head) Bill Gates now owns your content -- and you pay him every year," McNealy said.

However the new choice -- writing in Internet-based HTML (hyper-text mark-up link) format -- does not necessarily mean more sales for Sun, he said: "You could go to HTML and never buy one Sun computer in your life."

And Sun's vision of networks of relatively simple processors replacing some "hairball" complex personal computers did not pose a threat to the future of Microsoft or Intel, he said, stressing that Sun initially targets the corporate market.
"Microsoft doesn't have to fail for us to win in this part of the market," he said, describing a Windows/Intel personal computer as an "activity generator" rather than a "productivity generator."

But he said Sun's Java office suites -- cheap packages containing word processors, spreadsheets, presentation graphics and so on and due to be shipped this summer -- would challenge Microsoft, by changing the pricing model for office suites.
He cited prices around $250-400 per Microsoft suite versus $2-10 for the Java version, which runs on any computer.
"We're trying to make the desktop operating system a negative value-add," he said. "Microsoft makes another bag of money on desktop operating systems."
Still, the PC model of computing would still be around 20 years from now, he said: "Some people still ride horses."

And Sun's revenue flows do not depend entirely on its network concept at PC-level, he said. Smart cards and other embedded chip technologies like televisions, cellphones, cars and so on are a clear outlet for Java architecture.
"Seventy percent of the manufacturing volume of smart cards are putting the Java architecture -- the Java card architecture -- onto their smart card," he said.
Referring to the unit volumes of sales of such consumer electronic items, like televisions, he said: "If we never replaced one PC ... my shareholders will be very happy with us."
He also dismissed reports suggesting Java suffered from similar network security problems as those that have emerged in Microsoft's challenger to Java, ActiveX.
"(Such claims) couldn't be further from the truth," he said.
((-- Sara Henley, +358 9 490 649; sara.henley@reuters.com))
